claims.text: The initial as-cast eutectic high-entropy alloy has a fine FCC+B2 dual-phase lamellar microstructure.
A controlled thermomechanical treatment involving annealing, possibly after pre-deformation, can produce phase-selective recrystallization.
The treatment preferentially recrystallizes the soft FCC phase while preserving the hard B2 phase.
Appropriate annealing temperature and time can fully recrystallize the soft phase.
The predicted benefit should hold under room-temperature quasi-static tensile loading.
Phase-selective recrystallization produces a fully recrystallized soft phase embedded within the skeleton of a hard phase.
In the proposed alloy, the recrystallized soft phase is FCC and the continuous hard skeleton is B2.
Selective recrystallization eliminates weak boundaries in the eutectic microstructure.
Eliminating weak boundaries releases or enhances the strain-hardening capacity of the duplex phases.
The retained hard phase sustains the alloy's overall strength.
The phase-selectively recrystallized microstructure improves strain partitioning between the soft and hard phases.
Improved strain partitioning delays crack initiation and propagation.
The treatment can overcome the usual strength-ductility trade-off in eutectic high-entropy alloys.
The treated alloy will have higher yield strength than the as-cast lamellar baseline.
The treated alloy will have greater tensile ductility than the as-cast lamellar baseline.
A phase-selectively recrystallized eutectic high-entropy alloy can attain approximately 35% uniform elongation.
A phase-selectively recrystallized eutectic high-entropy alloy can combine approximately 35% uniform elongation with approximately 2 GPa true stress.
Composition, casting route, and testing regime are to remain unchanged between treated and baseline samples.
The exact annealing temperature, duration, and pre-deformation conditions required for ideal phase-selective recrystallization are not yet defined.
Failure to obtain both a statistically significant strength increase and a statistically significant ductility increase relative to an as-cast control would falsify the hypothesis.
